21.18: Then Manasseh died and was buried in his own garden—the Garden of Uzza. His son Amon took the throne next.
21.19: Amon was 22 when he became king, and he ruled for just two years in Jerusalem. His mama was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz from Jotbah.
21.20: He was no better than his daddy—evil in the Lord's eyes.
21.21: He followed Manasseh's ways, worshiping the same idols.
21.22: He completely turned his back on the Lord and refused to walk in His ways.
21.23: Then his own servants plotted against him and assassinated him in his palace.
21.24: But the people of Judah weren't having that—they executed everyone who was part of the conspiracy and made Amon's son Josiah king.
21.25: Everything else Amon did? It's in the book of the kings of Judah.
21.26: They buried him in his tomb in the Garden of Uzza, and then Josiah took the throne.

22.1: Josiah was just 8 years old when he became king, and he ruled for 31 years in Jerusalem. His mama was Jedidah, daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath.
22.2: He did right by the Lord, following in the ways of his ancestor David. He stayed solid—never strayed left or right.
22.3: In the 18th year of Josiah's reign, he sent Shaphan the scribe—son of Azaliah, grandson of Meshullam—to the temple with a message.
22.4: 'Go see Hilkiah, the high priest, and tell him to count all the money that's been collected at the Lord's house—the money the doorkeepers gathered from the people.'
22.5: 'Then give that money to the workers—the folks repairing the temple. Make sure the overseers hand it out to the carpenters, builders, and masons.'
22.6: 'Use it to buy timber and cut stone to fix up the Lord's house.'
22.7: 'Oh, and don't worry about making them report back on spending. These guys are trustworthy.'
22.8: Then Hilkiah the high priest told Shaphan, 'Yo, I found the Book of the Law in the Lord's house!' He handed it to Shaphan, and Shaphan started reading it.
22.9: Shaphan went back to the king and said, 'We handled the money from the temple and gave it to the workers overseeing the repairs.'
22.10: Then he added, 'By the way, Hilkiah the priest gave me this book.' And he started reading it to the king.
22.11: As soon as Josiah heard the words from the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes in distress.
22.12: Then he told Hilkiah, Ahikam (son of Shaphan), Achbor (son of Michaiah), Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah (one of his officials),
22.13: 'Go ask the Lord what this means for me, for the people, and for all Judah. The Lord's anger must be huge, 'cause our ancestors straight-up ignored this book. They didn't do what's written in it.'
22.14: So Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to see Huldah, the prophetess—the wife of Shallum (son of Tikvah, grandson of Harhas), the wardrobe keeper. She lived in Jerusalem's Second Quarter.
22.15: Huldah told them, 'The Lord God of Israel says this—go tell the king who sent you:'
22.16: 'The Lord says: I'm about to bring disaster on this place and its people—everything written in that book the king just heard.'
22.17: 'Why? 'Cause they turned their backs on Me, burned incense to other gods, and made Me furious with all their idol-worshiping ways. My anger against this place is set—I ain't holding it back.'
22.18: 'But for King Josiah, who sent y'all to ask about Me—tell him this:'
22.19: 'Since your heart was humble, and you truly listened when you heard My warning about this place becoming cursed and desolate—since you tore your clothes and cried out to Me—I heard you.'
22.20: 'So here's what I'm gonna do—I'll let you live out your days in peace. You won't have to see the disaster I'm bringing to this place.' So the officials took that message back to the king.

23.1: King Josiah gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.
23.2: Then he and all the people—priests, prophets, everybody from the richest to the poorest—went to the Lord's temple. And right there, Josiah read every word from the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the temple.
23.3: Then the king stood by the pillar and made a promise before the Lord—to follow Him, keep His commandments, and live by everything written in the book. And the people stood with him on that promise.
23.4: Josiah ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the assistant priests, and the temple guards to take everything made for Baal, Asherah, and the stars out of the Lord's house. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron, then took the ashes to Bethel.
23.5: He got rid of all those fake priests—the ones past kings had put in place to burn incense at the high places in Judah and Jerusalem. That included the ones burning incense to Baal, the sun, the moon, the constellations, and all the stars.
23.6: He even took the Asherah pole out of the Lord's house, burned it by the Brook Kidron, ground it to dust, and scattered the ashes over the graves of common folks.
23.7: Then he tore down the temple booths where the cult prostitutes were staying—those places where women wove cloth for the Asherah idol.
23.8: Josiah brought all the priests back from Judah's cities and shut down the high places, from Geba to Beersheba, where priests had been burning incense. He also destroyed the high places by the city gates—like the one at the entrance of Joshua's gate, the former governor of the city.
23.9: Even though these priests weren't allowed to serve at the Lord's altar in Jerusalem, they could still eat unleavened bread with the others.
23.10: Josiah shut down Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom so that nobody could burn their sons or daughters as sacrifices to Molech anymore.
23.11: He removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun. They were kept near the entrance of the Lord's temple, by the room of Nathan-Melech (a royal official). Then Josiah burned the chariots of the sun.
23.12: He tore down the altars on the roof of Ahaz's upper chamber that past kings of Judah had built, plus the ones Manasseh had built in the temple courts. He crushed them to dust and dumped the remains in the Brook Kidron.
23.13: Then he destroyed the high places east of Jerusalem on the south side of the Mount of Corruption. These were the spots Solomon had built for Ashtoreth (the Sidonian idol), Chemosh (the Moabite god), and Milcom (the Ammonite idol).
23.14: Josiah smashed the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and covered the places with human bones to make them unclean.
23.15: Even the altar at Bethel—the one Jeroboam, son of Nebat, had set up to lead Israel into sin—Josiah tore it down. He burned the high place, crushed it to dust, and burned the Asherah pole there too.
23.16: As Josiah looked around, he saw some tombs on the hill, had the bones dug up, and burned them on the altar to defile it—just like the man of God had prophesied years before.
23.17: Then Josiah asked, 'What's that gravestone over there?' The people said, 'That's the tomb of the man of God who prophesied what you just did to this altar.'
23.18: Josiah said, 'Leave him be. Don't touch his bones.' So they left his bones, along with the bones of the prophet from Samaria.
23.19: Josiah wiped out all the shrines in Samaria that past Israelite kings had built to provoke God. He destroyed them just like he did in Bethel.
23.20: Then he executed all the pagan priests in Samaria and burned their bones on the altars. After that, he went back to Jerusalem.
23.21: Josiah told all the people, 'We celebrating the Passover for the Lord, just like it says in the Book of the Covenant.'
23.22: A Passover like this hadn't been celebrated since the time of the judges—not even under the kings of Israel or Judah.
23.23: But in the 18th year of Josiah's reign, he made sure the Passover was properly celebrated in Jerusalem.
23.24: Josiah also removed all the psychics, fortune tellers, household idols, and any detestable thing in Judah and Jerusalem. He made sure to follow everything written in the Book of the Law that Hilkiah the priest had found in the Lord's temple.
23.25: No king before Josiah had ever turned to the Lord with his whole heart, soul, and strength like he did—following the Law of Moses completely. And no king after him did either.
23.26: But even with all that, the Lord's anger against Judah was still hot—because of all the evil Manasseh had done before.
23.27: The Lord said, 'Judah's getting the same treatment as Israel. I'm removing them from My sight and rejecting this city, Jerusalem—the place I chose for My name to dwell.'
23.28: Everything else Josiah did? It's all written in the book of the kings of Judah.
23.29: During Josiah's reign, Pharaoh Necho of Egypt marched to the Euphrates River to help the king of Assyria. Josiah went out to fight him, but Necho killed him at Megiddo.
23.30: Josiah's servants carried his body in a chariot back to Jerusalem and buried him in his own tomb. Then the people took his son, Jehoahaz, anointed him, and made him king.
23.31: Jehoahaz was 23 when he became king, but he only lasted three months in Jerusalem. His mama was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
23.32: And like his ancestors, he did evil in the Lord's sight.
23.33: Then Pharaoh Necho locked him up at Riblah in Hamath so he couldn't rule in Jerusalem. And he put Judah under a heavy tax—100 talents of silver and 1 talent of gold.
23.34: Necho then replaced Jehoahaz with his brother Eliakim, son of Josiah, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Meanwhile, he took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died.
23.35: Jehoiakim paid the silver and gold to Pharaoh by taxing the people—each person had to pay their share according to the king's demands.
23.36: Jehoiakim was 25 when he became king, and he ruled for 11 years in Jerusalem. His mama was Zebudah, daughter of Pedaiah from Rumah.
23.37: And just like his ancestors, he did evil in the Lord's sight.

24.1: During Jehoiakim's reign, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came through, and Jehoiakim had no choice but to serve him for three years. But then, Jehoiakim got bold and rebelled.
24.2: So the Lord sent raiders—Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites—straight at Judah to tear it apart, just like He warned through His prophets.
24.3: This was all part of God's judgment. Judah was getting removed from His sight because of the sins of Manasseh—dude had done too much wrong.
24.4: Especially for all the innocent blood he shed. He filled Jerusalem with it, and the Lord wasn't letting that slide.
24.5: Everything else Jehoiakim did? It's all written in the book of the kings of Judah.
24.6: Then Jehoiakim died, and his son Jehoiachin took over.
24.7: Meanwhile, the king of Egypt stayed out of it, 'cause the king of Babylon had already taken all his land—from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River.
24.8: Jehoiachin was 18 when he became king, but he only ruled for three months in Jerusalem. His mama was Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan from Jerusalem.
24.9: And just like his daddy, he did evil in the Lord's sight.
24.10: Around that time, Babylon's army came up against Jerusalem and laid siege to the city.
24.11: Then Nebuchadnezzar himself showed up while his men were surrounding the city.
24.12: So Jehoiachin, his mama, his officials, his commanders, and his officers all surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar. In the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, he took Jehoiachin prisoner.
24.13: Babylon's king looted everything—he emptied out the Lord's temple and the royal treasury. He even cut apart all the gold items Solomon had made for the temple, just like the Lord had warned.
24.14: Then he exiled the entire city—captains, warriors, 10,000 captives, plus all the craftsmen and metalworkers. Only the poorest folks got left behind.
24.15: Jehoiachin, his mama, his wives, his officials, and the upper-class citizens were all taken to Babylon.
24.16: Nebuchadnezzar also took 7,000 elite soldiers and 1,000 skilled workers—anybody fit for war—into captivity.
24.17: Then the king of Babylon made Mattaniah (Jehoiachin's uncle) the new king and changed his name to Zedekiah.
24.18: Zedekiah was 21 when he became king, and he ruled for 11 years in Jerusalem. His mama was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
24.19: But he wasn't any better—he did evil, just like Jehoiakim.
24.20: At this point, God's anger was fully on Jerusalem and Judah. He finally cast them out of His presence. But even after all that, Zedekiah still tried to rebel against Babylon.

25.1: In the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his whole army came through and surrounded Jerusalem. They built a siege wall all around it.
25.2: The city stayed under siege until the eleventh year of Zedekiah's reign.
25.3: By the ninth day of the fourth month, the famine was so bad there was no food left for the people.
25.4: Then the city walls got breached. That night, Judah's warriors tried to escape through the gate near the king's garden, even though Babylon's army had the whole city surrounded. Zedekiah took off through the plains.
25.5: But Babylon's army chased him down and caught him in the plains of Jericho. His whole army scattered.
25.6: They captured Zedekiah and took him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, where they handed down judgment on him.
25.7: Right in front of Zedekiah, they killed his sons. Then they blinded him, put him in chains, and hauled him off to Babylon.
25.8: On the seventh day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the Babylonian guard, came to Jerusalem.
25.9: He burned down the Lord's temple, the king's palace, and every important building in Jerusalem.
25.10: Then the Babylonian army tore down the city walls.
25.11: Nebuzaradan took into captivity the rest of the people who were still in the city, including those who had already surrendered to Babylon.
25.12: But he left behind some of the poorest folks to work the vineyards and fields.
25.13: Babylon's army broke apart the bronze pillars, the carts, and the massive bronze basin (the 'Sea') in the Lord's temple and took all the bronze back to Babylon.
25.14: They also took the pots, shovels, trimmers, spoons, and all the bronze tools the priests used for worship.
25.15: Anything made of gold or silver—firepans, basins, you name it—Nebuzaradan took it all.
25.16: The sheer amount of bronze in the two pillars, the Sea, and the carts Solomon had made for the temple was massive.
25.17: Each pillar was 27 feet tall, with a 4.5-foot-high bronze capital on top, decorated with bronze pomegranates woven into a network. Both pillars were the same.
25.18: Nebuzaradan also arrested Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and three temple guards.
25.19: He took the city's army commander, five of the king's closest officials still in the city, the chief recruiting officer, and 60 other men who were still in Jerusalem.
25.20: Nebuzaradan rounded them up and took them to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah.
25.21: There, the king of Babylon had them all executed. And just like that, Judah was officially taken into captivity.
25.22: Nebuchadnezzar put Gedaliah, son of Ahikam (son of Shaphan), in charge of the people left in Judah.
25.23: When Judah's army commanders and their men heard Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, they went to meet him at Mizpah: Ishmael (son of Nethaniah), Johanan (son of Kareah), Seraiah (son of Tanhumeth), Jaazaniah, and others.
25.24: Gedaliah told them, 'Don't be scared of serving Babylon. Stay in the land, serve the king of Babylon, and things will go well for y'all.'
25.25: But in the seventh month, Ishmael (son of Nethaniah, from the royal family) and ten men with him assassinated Gedaliah, along with the Jews and Babylonians who were with him at Mizpah.
25.26: After that, everyone—rich and poor, along with Judah's army leaders—fled to Egypt, scared of what Babylon might do next.
25.27: In the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, Evil-Merodach, king of Babylon, took the throne and decided to free Jehoiachin.
25.28: He treated him kindly and gave him a better position than the other captive kings in Babylon.
25.29: Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and ate at the king's table regularly for the rest of his life.
25.30: And for the rest of his days, the king of Babylon made sure Jehoiachin got a daily allowance of food.
